reports.title: Market Insight: AI Is Reshaping MDR Pricing, but Most Vendors Aren't Ready
reports.summary: Agentic AI is changing the cost structure and value delivery of MDR services, yet most providers have not adjusted their pricing models to reflect this shift. Outcome-based pricing remains underadopted despite clear market signals that buyers want measurable results.
reports.spa: By 2028, 40% of MDR contracts will include at least one outcome-linked pricing component tied to measurable security improvements, up from less than 5% today. Vendors that fail to develop outcome-based commercial models by 2027 will face a structural competitive disadvantage in retention and new business.

findings.header: Outcome-based pricing adoption is very low across the MDR market.
findings.body: Of 95 vendors assessed, the average score for success and outcome-linked fee structures (PRC-SUC) is just 1.63 out of 5.0, with 82 vendors (86%) scoring 2.0 or below. Only two vendors score above 3.0 on this dimension. The median score is 1 (the lowest possible), indicating that most MDR providers have made no meaningful progress toward tying commercial terms to measurable client outcomes.

findings.header: AI-mature vendors show measurably higher pricing sophistication.
findings.body: Vendors with Significant or higher AI pricing influence (19 providers) average 2.86 across all pricing dimensions versus 1.84 for Minimal-influence vendors (27 providers), a 1.02-point gap on a 5-point scale. This correlation holds across every pricing dimension but is most pronounced in outcome alignment (PRC-OUT), where AI-mature vendors score 2.58 versus 1.04 for Minimal-tier providers.

findings.header: The market misunderstands what outcome-based pricing means.
findings.body: Most vendors equate "outcomes" with SLA uptime guarantees or basic breach notification speeds. True outcome-based pricing ties commercial terms to measurable security improvements: reduction in mean time to detect (MTTD), mean time to respond (MTTR), quantifiable risk posture improvements, or incident frequency reduction commitments backed by financial mechanisms such as breach warranties or performance-based fee adjustments.

findings.header: Composable pricing models are a prerequisite for outcome-based evolution, but two-thirds of vendors remain subscription-only.
findings.body: 64 of 95 vendors (67%) operate on pure subscription models, scoring an average of just 1.34 on PRC-SUC. The 27 composable-model vendors average 2.41 on the same dimension, nearly double. Outcome-based pricing requires the modularity and flexibility that subscription-only models cannot support.

findings.header: AI is creating an efficiency dividend that vendors are capturing rather than sharing with buyers.
findings.body: As AI-driven automation reduces the per-incident cost of detection and response, vendors are improving their margins without passing those efficiency gains through to clients via adjusted pricing mechanisms. The absence of usage-based alignment (PRC-USG averages just 2.14/5.0) means buyers have no visibility into how AI-driven efficiency improvements affect the cost of their service.

findings.header: The pricing maturity gap between leaders and laggards is widening, driven primarily by AI adoption differences.
findings.body: The top-10 vendors by overall pricing score average 3.65/5.0 while the market average is 2.35/5.0, a 1.30-point spread. The top performers uniformly show higher AI influence scores (averaging 3.5+), composable pricing models, and at least nascent outcome-linked commercial terms. This gap will widen as AI-first vendors use efficiency gains to fund outcome guarantees that subscription-only providers cannot match.

recommendations.header: Redefine outcome-based pricing in concrete, measurable terms.
recommendations.body: Product leaders must move beyond SLA guarantees and establish commercial structures tied to quantifiable security outcomes (MTTD/MTTR improvement commitments, coverage expansion metrics, incident frequency reduction targets, and risk score improvements) backed by financial mechanisms such as breach warranties, performance credits, or shared-savings arrangements. Start with a single outcome metric tied to a fee adjustment and expand from there.

recommendations.header: Build an AI efficiency-sharing pricing layer that demonstrates value to buyers.
recommendations.body: Establish transparent mechanisms (efficiency dashboards, cost-per-incident trending, or AI utilization reporting) that show buyers how AI-driven automation is reducing service delivery costs. Tie at least a portion of pricing to these efficiency metrics through consumption-based components or graduated discount structures. Vendors that share the AI dividend early will secure longer contract terms and higher retention.

recommendations.header: Transition from subscription-only to composable pricing architectures.
recommendations.body: Begin decomposing monolithic subscription tiers into modular service components (base detection, response orchestration, threat hunting, incident retainer, and outcome guarantees) that buyers can assemble based on their specific risk profile. Our data shows composable vendors score 2.80 versus 2.16 for subscription-only across all pricing dimensions (a 30% premium), and the gap on outcome-linked pricing is even wider (2.41 vs. 1.34).

recommendations.header: Invest in AI pricing-influence capabilities as a direct commercial differentiator.
recommendations.body: The 1.02-point pricing sophistication gap between AI-mature and AI-minimal vendors is the single strongest predictor of overall pricing model maturity. Product leaders should treat AI investment not just as a cost efficiency play but as the enabler of commercial model innovation, from usage-based billing driven by AI workload telemetry to outcome guarantees underwritten by AI-validated detection capabilities.

recommendations.header: Develop a phased roadmap from transparency to outcomes, anchored to AI maturity milestones.
recommendations.body: Most vendors cannot leap directly from subscription-only pricing to full outcome-based models. The progression should follow a clear sequence: (1) publish transparent pricing and tier definitions, (2) introduce usage-aligned components tied to data volume or endpoint count, (3) add composable modules with mix-and-match flexibility, (4) introduce limited outcome commitments (e.g., MTTR guarantees with service credits), and (5) implement full risk-sharing or performance-linked fee structures. Each stage should be unlocked by corresponding AI capability maturity.

recommendations.header: Establish competitive pricing intelligence as a standing practice, not a periodic exercise.
recommendations.body: With a 1.30-point spread between top-10 and market-average pricing scores, and AI influence accelerating the divergence, vendors operating without structured pricing benchmarking are flying blind. Product leaders should institute quarterly pricing model assessments that benchmark their position on each pricing dimension against the market, track the velocity of competitor pricing evolution, and identify the specific AI capabilities driving commercial model changes in leading vendors.

analysis_sections.title: What Outcome-Based Pricing Actually Means, and Why the Market Gets It Wrong
analysis_sections.body:
The term "outcome-based pricing" has become a marketing fixture in managed detection and response. Vendors routinely cite SLA-backed response times or uptime guarantees as evidence of outcome alignment. This misrepresents what outcome-based pricing requires.

True outcome-based pricing establishes a direct financial link between what the buyer pays and the measurable security outcomes they receive. This means commercial terms that adjust, up or down, based on metrics the buyer actually cares about: How fast are threats detected and contained? Is the organization's attack surface actually shrinking? Are incidents becoming less frequent, less severe, or both? Is the cost of security per unit of business value improving over time?

In practice, this can take several forms:

- **Breach warranties**: Financial guarantees that pay out if a covered breach occurs, underwritten by the vendor's confidence in their detection and response capabilities.
- **Performance-linked fee adjustments**: Pricing that flexes based on achieved MTTD/MTTR improvements, with defined baselines and measurement periods.
- **Risk-score-tied subscriptions**: Pricing tied to an independently measured risk posture score, where improvement reduces the fee and degradation increases it.
- **Shared savings models**: Arrangements where a portion of the vendor's fee is tied to demonstrated cost avoidance or efficiency improvements for the buyer.
- **Incident severity caps**: Commercial terms that cap the buyer's financial exposure for incidents above a defined severity threshold.

Our assessment of 95 MDR vendors found that PRC-SUC (success and outcome fees) is the weakest pricing dimension in the market, averaging just 1.63 out of 5.0, nearly half the score of subscription transparency (3.52). The median is 1.0, meaning the typical MDR vendor has no outcome-linked pricing mechanism whatsoever. Even among the top 10 vendors on this dimension, the average is only 3.20, indicating that even leaders are in early stages. The two vendors that score above 3.0 on PRC-SUC, Accenture Security and Deloitte Cyber, are both large consultancies with composable models, not pureplay MDR providers.

analysis_sections.title: Why Outcome-Based Pricing Adoption Lags So Far Behind
analysis_sections.body:
Several structural and organizational factors explain the sluggish adoption of outcome-based pricing, despite clear buyer demand:

**1. Lack of measurement infrastructure.** Outcome-based pricing requires metrics that both parties trust. Most MDR providers lack the telemetry, benchmarking, and reporting infrastructure to measure and attribute outcomes with enough rigor to tie commercial terms to them. Without normalized baselines for MTTD, MTTR, incident frequency, or coverage breadth, outcome commitments cannot be quantified.

**2. Revenue predictability addiction.** Subscription-only models provide smooth, predictable revenue streams that are rewarded by investors and simplify financial planning. Outcome-based components introduce variability into the revenue model, which finance teams and boards resist. 64 of 95 vendors (67%) remain subscription-only, and their average overall pricing score of 2.16 (versus 2.80 for composable vendors) indicates that the subscription model itself constrains pricing sophistication.

**3. Insufficient AI capability to underwrite guarantees.** Outcome-based pricing requires confidence in delivery. A vendor cannot offer a breach warranty or MTTR guarantee without the AI-driven detection and response capabilities to consistently achieve them. Our data shows this directly: vendors with Significant AI influence score 2.16 on PRC-SUC versus 1.04 for Minimal-tier vendors. AI maturity is the prerequisite for outcome pricing.

**4. Misaligned organizational incentives.** In many MDR providers, pricing decisions are owned by finance or product management teams that optimize for margin protection, not by security operations teams that understand what outcomes are achievable. This creates a structural disconnect where the people closest to delivery have the least influence on commercial model design.

**5. Fear of accountability.** Outcome-linked pricing makes vendor performance transparent and has real consequences. If a provider commits to a 30-minute MTTR on critical incidents and fails, the financial penalty is immediate and visible. Many vendors prefer the opacity of flat-rate subscriptions where poor performance is masked and contract renewals are a commercial negotiation rather than a performance evaluation.

**6. Legacy contract structures.** Existing multi-year subscription contracts create inertia. Migrating a large installed base from flat-rate subscriptions to outcome-linked models requires renegotiating hundreds of contracts, retraining sales teams, and rebuilding billing systems, a transformation most vendors underestimate.

analysis_sections.title: AI Is Changing the Cost Equation, but Buyers Aren't Seeing It
analysis_sections.body:
Agentic AI is sharply reducing the per-incident cost of MDR service delivery. Automated triage, AI-accelerated threat hunting, machine-driven response playbooks, and predictive detection are enabling vendors to handle more volume with fewer human analysts. This should, in theory, create a natural transition toward efficiency-sharing or outcome-aligned pricing: the vendor delivers more value at lower cost, and the buyer shares in that efficiency gain.

Instead, most vendors are capturing the AI efficiency dividend entirely as margin improvement. The market average for usage-based alignment (PRC-USG) is just 2.14 out of 5.0, meaning most vendors have no mechanism for buyers to see, let alone benefit from, AI-driven cost reductions. The buyer pays the same subscription fee whether their incidents are handled by a senior analyst spending hours on manual investigation or by an AI agent that resolves the same alert in minutes.

This will not hold. As buyers become more informed about AI capabilities and costs, they will demand transparency into how AI efficiency affects what they pay. The 19 vendors in the Significant AI influence tier (averaging 2.86 across all pricing dimensions versus 1.84 for the Minimal tier) are beginning to build this transparency through AI workload dashboards, cost-per-incident reporting, and graduated pricing tiers that reflect AI utilization. These vendors are not more generous; they are more strategic. By sharing the efficiency dividend early, they build a competitive advantage rooted in trust, transparency, and demonstrable value that subscription-only providers cannot replicate.

analysis_sections.title: The Composable Model Imperative
analysis_sections.body:
The data reveals a clear structural prerequisite for pricing model evolution: composability. Vendors with composable pricing models, where buyers can assemble service packages from modular components, score 2.80 across all pricing dimensions versus 2.16 for subscription-only providers. On the critical PRC-SUC dimension, the gap is even starker: 2.41 versus 1.34.

This is not coincidental. Outcome-based pricing components cannot be bolted onto a flat-rate subscription. They require the architectural flexibility to price different service layers differently: a base detection fee, a response orchestration component, an outcome guarantee overlay, a shared-savings mechanism. Each layer has distinct cost drivers, risk profiles, and measurement requirements.

The 27 composable vendors (28% of the market) are positioned to add outcome-linked components over time. The 64 subscription-only vendors (67%) face a structural rebuild before outcomes can even be priced. As AI continues to change how MDR services are delivered, this divide will widen into a lasting competitive gap.

reports.background:
The managed detection and response (MDR) market has seen considerable consolidation and commoditization pressure over the past three years. As core detection and response capabilities have become table stakes, pricing has emerged as a primary competitive battleground and a key indicator of vendor positioning.

This assessment evaluated 95 MDR service providers across six pricing dimensions: subscription transparency (PRC-SUB), usage-based alignment (PRC-USG), fixed delivery pricing (PRC-FIX), success and outcome fees (PRC-SUC), composability and model maturity (PRC-COM), and pricing-to-outcomes alignment (PRC-OUT). Each dimension was scored on a 1-5 scale based on evidence from vendor documentation, publicly available pricing information, and contracted engagement terms.

The overall market average pricing maturity score of 2.35 out of 5.0 places the MDR market in the "developing" stage. The strongest dimension, subscription transparency at 3.52, reflects an industry that has reached basic commercial maturity in publishing clear tier structures and feature sets. Every other dimension falls below 3.0, with the two outcome-related dimensions (PRC-SUC at 1.63 and PRC-OUT at 1.77) trailing well behind.

The AI enrichment layer, which assesses how AI operational maturity influences pricing model sophistication, reveals that 0 of 95 vendors reach the Transformative tier, 19 are Significant, 49 are Emerging, and 27 are Minimal. The market average AI pricing influence score of 2.48 out of 5.0 confirms that the industry has not yet translated AI investment into commercial model innovation at scale.
reports.impact:
The implications of this pricing maturity deficit are direct and practical for both MDR providers and the organizations they serve.

**For MDR vendors,** the inability to articulate and deliver outcome-based pricing will become a serious competitive problem within the next two to three years. As AI-first vendors use efficiency gains to fund outcome guarantees (breach warranties, MTTR commitments, risk-score-linked pricing), providers that cannot match these commercial structures will compete solely on price and feature lists. This is a losing position in a commoditizing market. The 1.02-point pricing sophistication gap between AI-mature and AI-minimal vendors is already visible in win rates and retention, and it will grow.

**For buyers,** the slow adoption of outcome-based pricing means they continue to bear the full risk of poor vendor performance. A subscription-only MDR contract provides no financial consequence if the vendor fails to detect a breach, responds slowly, or delivers inconsistent coverage. Buyers should actively seek vendors willing to put commercial terms against measurable outcomes, and treat a vendor's refusal to do so as a signal about their confidence in their own capabilities.

**For the broader cybersecurity services market,** the MDR pricing evolution is a leading indicator of a market-wide shift. As AI transforms cost structures across managed security services, the pressure for outcome-aligned pricing will extend to SOC-as-a-Service, vulnerability management, and security consulting. Vendors that develop outcome-based commercial capabilities in MDR will have a transferable advantage across their portfolio.

The platform MDR providers (28 vendors, averaging 2.43 and the highest AI influence at 2.75) are best positioned to lead this transition. Their technology platform investments provide the telemetry infrastructure needed to measure outcomes, and their AI adoption is creating the efficiency surplus needed to fund outcome guarantees. IR-enhanced MDR providers (7 vendors, 2.64 average) have the highest pricing maturity but may be constrained by their smaller scale and incident-dependent revenue streams.

Pureplay MDR providers (15 vendors, averaging 2.14 with the lowest AI influence at 2.13) face the most significant challenge. Without the AI capability to underwrite outcome commitments or the platform telemetry to measure them, pureplay vendors risk being squeezed between platform providers offering outcome guarantees at competitive prices and niche specialists offering deep expertise at premium rates.
reports.conclusion:
The MDR pricing picture shows a market in transition that has not yet arrived. Subscription transparency is reasonably mature, but outcome-based pricing, the dimension that matters most to buyers, is essentially absent. With 86% of vendors scoring 2.0 or below on success and outcome fees, and a median score of 1.0, the market is not incrementally behind; it has barely started.

AI adoption is the single most predictive variable in pricing model sophistication. The 1.02-point gap between AI-mature and AI-minimal vendors, and the even wider divergence on outcome-specific dimensions (2.58 vs. 1.04 on PRC-OUT), make clear that AI capability is not just correlated with pricing innovation; it enables it. Vendors cannot credibly commit to outcome-based pricing without the AI-driven detection, response, and measurement capabilities to consistently deliver against those commitments.

The path forward requires three parallel investments: AI capability maturity (to underwrite outcome guarantees), pricing architecture modernization (from subscription-only to composable), and measurement infrastructure (to enable transparent, trust-based outcome metrics). Vendors that treat pricing model evolution as a finance exercise rather than a capability development effort will find themselves unable to compete as the market matures.

Product leaders should not wait for buyer pressure to force this transition. The vendors that move first, establishing outcome-linked commercial terms while competitors stick with subscription-only models, will set the standard for what "good" looks like and make it harder for followers to catch up. The data is clear: AI maturity enables pricing innovation, pricing innovation enables competitive differentiation, and competitive differentiation determines long-term market position.

reports.title: MDR Pricing Won't Be Revolutionized by Agentic AI
reports.summary: Industry hype is forcing product teams to develop arbitrary Agentic AI products that don't measure up to expectations. Product teams replacing SOAR automation with AI is dominating the MDR space with the illusion that this is providing additional value and outcomes that will drive revenue growth.
reports.spa: By 2028, fewer than 15% of MDR providers will have shipped a pricing model where AI-driven capabilities directly change what the customer pays, despite over 80% claiming AI integration in their product marketing. Product teams that confuse AI feature presence with AI pricing influence will lose share to vendors whose roadmaps connect AI investment to measurable commercial differentiation.

findings.header: Product teams are shipping AI features that don't move the pricing needle.
findings.body: Of 95 MDR vendors assessed, the average AI pricing influence score is just 2.48/5.0, and zero vendors reach the Transformative tier. 49 vendors (52%) sit at Emerging, meaning they have added AI features to their detection or triage pipeline but have not connected those capabilities to pricing model changes. Product investment in AI is high; product impact on commercial models is near zero.

findings.header: SOAR-to-AI relabeling is the dominant product pattern, and it isn't working.
findings.body: Most MDR product teams are replacing SOAR playbook automation with AI/ML-driven triage and response orchestration. The market treats this as innovation, but the data shows otherwise: the 49 Emerging-tier vendors (who have done exactly this) average just 2.20 across all pricing dimensions, barely above the 1.84 average for Minimal-tier vendors who have no AI at all. Swapping SOAR for AI without changing the commercial model produces the same subscription-only pricing at the same margins.

findings.body: Vendors with Significant AI influence score 2.86 across pricing dimensions versus 1.84 for Minimal. That gap exists because the Significant-tier vendors built AI into their product in ways that change what they can sell and how they can price it: usage-based billing on AI workload volume, outcome guarantees underwritten by AI detection confidence, composable modules enabled by AI-driven service decomposition. The product decisions drove the commercial differentiation.

findings.header: Outcome-based pricing (PRC-SUC at 1.63/5.0) is a product capability gap, not a sales problem.
findings.body: Product leaders often treat pricing as a go-to-market concern. But outcome-linked pricing requires product capabilities that most MDR platforms lack: normalized outcome measurement and reporting, confidence-scored detection that can underwrite SLA commitments, and modular service architecture that separates base detection from outcome guarantee overlays. Until product builds these capabilities, sales has nothing to price against.

findings.header: Two-thirds of vendors are locked into subscription-only models because of product architecture, not commercial preference.
findings.body: 64 of 95 vendors (67%) operate subscription-only pricing. The root cause is monolithic product architecture: a single detection-and-response pipeline delivered as a flat service. Without product-level decomposition into separately measurable, separately deliverable components, pricing teams cannot create composable or outcome-linked tiers even if they want to. Composable vendors score 2.80 vs. 2.16 for subscription-only on overall pricing maturity.

findings.header: The top-10 pricing leaders all made deliberate product architecture choices that enabled their commercial models.
findings.body: The top-10 vendors by pricing score average 3.65/5.0 versus the market average of 2.35. Every one of them has (a) a composable or hybrid pricing model, (b) Significant or higher AI influence, and (c) at least one measurable outcome metric exposed to customers. Product teams that don't make equivalent architectural investments now will not be able to compete on pricing in 2027-2028.

recommendations.header: Stop treating AI as a feature checkbox and start treating it as a pricing architecture enabler.
recommendations.body: Product roadmaps should tie every AI investment to a specific commercial model capability it unlocks. If an AI feature does not enable a new pricing dimension (usage-based metering, outcome measurement, confidence-scored SLAs, or modular service decomposition), question whether it belongs on the roadmap at all. The 1.02-point pricing gap between AI-mature and AI-minimal vendors is driven by AI that changes what you can sell, not AI that improves what you already deliver for free.

recommendations.header: Decompose the monolithic detection-and-response pipeline into separately priceable service components.
recommendations.body: The single biggest product architecture blocker to pricing innovation is the flat, bundled MDR service. Product teams should break the pipeline into discrete, measurable components: base detection and alerting, response orchestration, proactive threat hunting, outcome guarantee overlays, and efficiency reporting. Each component needs its own telemetry, its own SLA surface, and its own cost model. The data shows composable vendors outscore subscription-only by 30% across all pricing dimensions.

recommendations.header: Build outcome measurement into the product, not the dashboard.
recommendations.body: The reason PRC-SUC scores 1.63/5.0 across the market is that most products cannot measure outcomes in a way that supports commercial commitments. Product teams need to ship normalized MTTD/MTTR measurement, risk posture scoring, incident frequency tracking, and coverage breadth metrics as first-class product features with APIs, not as after-the-fact dashboard reports. Pricing cannot commit to outcomes that the product cannot measure and attribute.

recommendations.header: Replace the SOAR-to-AI migration with an AI-to-pricing pipeline.
recommendations.body: The current dominant product pattern (replace SOAR playbooks with AI orchestration) is a dead end for commercial differentiation. The next product investment should focus on connecting AI capabilities to pricing mechanics: AI workload telemetry that enables usage-based billing, AI detection confidence scores that underwrite MTTR guarantees, and AI efficiency metrics that support shared-savings pricing. If the AI doesn't change what you charge, it only changes your cost.

recommendations.header: Set a 12-month product milestone to enable at least one outcome-linked pricing component.
recommendations.body: Based on the progression from Minimal to Significant AI influence (a jump from 1.84 to 2.86 on pricing dimensions), product teams should target shipping the foundational capabilities for one outcome-linked pricing tier within 12 months. A reasonable first target: an MTTR guarantee with service credits, backed by AI-driven response orchestration and normalized measurement infrastructure. This single capability moves a vendor from the 86% stuck at PRC-SUC <= 2.0 into the competitive tier.

recommendations.header: Establish a quarterly product-pricing alignment review with commercial teams.
recommendations.body: The disconnect between product capability and commercial model is the core reason pricing innovation lags. Product leaders should institute a quarterly review where product roadmap milestones are mapped to specific pricing model changes they enable, pricing team feedback on commercial blockers is fed back into the product backlog, and competitor product-pricing moves are analyzed for architectural patterns to replicate or counter.

analysis_sections.title: The SOAR-to-AI Swap: Why Product Teams Are Building the Wrong Thing
analysis_sections.body:
The dominant product investment pattern in MDR over the past 18 months is straightforward: replace SOAR-based playbook automation with AI/ML-driven orchestration. Vendors are rewriting triage logic to use machine learning classifiers instead of rule trees, replacing manual investigation workflows with AI-assisted enrichment, and swapping static response playbooks with AI-driven decision engines.

The problem is not that this work is bad engineering. It often reduces mean time to triage, lowers false positive rates, and improves analyst efficiency. The problem is that none of these improvements show up in the commercial model. The vendor still sells a flat subscription. The customer still pays per-seat or per-endpoint. The AI reduces the vendor's cost of delivery without changing what the customer experiences commercially.

Our data makes this visible: the 49 Emerging-tier vendors (vendors that have shipped AI features but not connected them to pricing) average 2.20 across pricing dimensions. The 27 Minimal-tier vendors (no meaningful AI in pricing) average 1.84. That's a 0.36-point gap for all the AI investment. By contrast, the 19 Significant-tier vendors, who built AI in ways that change their commercial model, average 2.86, a full point above Emerging.

The takeaway for product leaders: shipping better AI is not enough. The AI has to change what you can sell.

analysis_sections.title: Product Architecture Is the Real Pricing Bottleneck
analysis_sections.body:
When product leaders ask why their pricing team can't offer composable or outcome-linked models, the answer is almost always product architecture. Consider what outcome-based pricing requires:

- **Normalized outcome metrics**: MTTD, MTTR, detection coverage, incident frequency. These need to be measured per-customer, with baselines, trending, and attribution. Most MDR products measure aggregate operational metrics for internal use, not per-customer outcome metrics for commercial use.

- **Modular service boundaries**: To price detection separately from response, or base service separately from outcome guarantees, the product must actually deliver these as separable components with independent SLAs and telemetry.

- **Confidence scoring**: To underwrite an MTTR guarantee or breach warranty, the product needs to express detection and response confidence in a way that actuaries (or at least finance teams) can model.

- **Usage telemetry**: To offer usage-based pricing components, the product needs metering infrastructure that tracks AI workload volume, incident complexity, and resource consumption at a per-customer level.

64 of 95 vendors lack these capabilities. Their product delivers MDR as a monolithic pipeline: alerts go in, validated incidents and responses come out. There is no internal boundary where a pricing team could insert a usage meter, an outcome metric, or a modular component boundary. The product architecture dictates subscription-only pricing, regardless of what the commercial team wants.

The 27 composable-model vendors have invested in product decomposition. Their 30% pricing premium (2.80 vs. 2.16) is not because their sales team is more creative. It's because their product team gave pricing something to work with.

analysis_sections.title: AI Efficiency Gains Are Going to Margin, Not to Product Differentiation
analysis_sections.body:
Product teams are improving operational efficiency with AI and reporting this as a product success. Triage time is down. Analyst-to-incident ratios are up. Cost per incident is falling. These are real improvements.

But from a product strategy perspective, efficiency gains that go entirely to margin are a wasted competitive asset. The 19 Significant-tier vendors are using AI efficiency data as product features: customer-facing AI workload dashboards, cost-per-incident trending reports, and transparent efficiency metrics that customers can see. These features become the foundation for pricing innovation because they give customers something to pay for (or pay less for) based on AI performance.

The market average for usage-based alignment (PRC-USG) is 2.14/5.0. This means most products do not expose any AI efficiency data to customers in a way that could support pricing changes. The product team captures the efficiency, finance captures the margin, and the customer sees no difference.

Product leaders who want to compete on pricing in 2027-2028 need to treat AI efficiency visibility as a product feature on the roadmap, not a back-office operational metric. The vendors who share this data with customers are building trust and commercial leverage that subscription-only competitors cannot match.

analysis_sections.title: The 12-Month Product Investment Window
analysis_sections.body:
The gap between the top-10 pricing leaders (3.65/5.0) and the market average (2.35) is 1.30 points and growing. The product decisions that enabled the leaders' pricing models were made 12-18 months before those models shipped. This means the investment window for mid-market vendors is now.

A realistic 12-month product roadmap for pricing enablement should target four milestones:

**Months 1-3: Outcome measurement infrastructure.** Ship per-customer MTTD/MTTR tracking, normalized baselines, and trending. This is the prerequisite for any outcome-linked pricing component and the capability most vendors lack.

**Months 3-6: Service decomposition.** Identify 2-3 modular boundaries in the MDR pipeline (e.g., base detection, response orchestration, threat hunting) and instrument each with independent telemetry and SLA surfaces.

**Months 6-9: AI efficiency exposure.** Build a customer-facing AI workload dashboard that shows AI triage rates, automation percentages, and cost efficiency trends. This becomes the pricing team's tool for usage-based and efficiency-sharing conversations.

**Months 9-12: First outcome-linked capability.** Ship an MTTR guarantee with service credits (or similar) on at least one tier, backed by the measurement infrastructure from months 1-3 and the AI detection confidence from the existing pipeline.

This sequence moves a vendor from the 86% stuck at PRC-SUC <= 2.0 to a position where outcome-linked pricing is at least available. The product investment is concrete, sequenced, and directly tied to commercial model impact.

reports.conclusion:
The MDR pricing data tells a product strategy story. The vendors with the highest pricing maturity are not the ones with the best sales teams or the most aggressive discounting. analysis_sections.title: What Outcome-Based Pricing Actually Means, and Why the Market Gets It Wrong
analysis_sections.body:
The term "outcome-based pricing" has become a marketing fixture in managed detection and response. Vendors routinely cite SLA-backed response times or uptime guarantees as evidence of outcome alignment. This misrepresents what outcome-based pricing requires.

True outcome-based pricing establishes a direct financial link between what the buyer pays and the measurable security outcomes they receive. This means commercial terms that adjust, up or down, based on metrics the buyer actually cares about: How fast are threats detected and contained? Is the organization's attack surface actually shrinking? Are incidents becoming less frequent, less severe, or both? Is the cost of security per unit of business value improving over time?

In practice, this can take several forms:

- **Breach warranties**: Financial guarantees that pay out if a covered breach occurs, underwritten by the vendor's confidence in their detection and response capabilities.
- **Performance-linked fee adjustments**: Pricing that flexes based on achieved detection and response time improvements, with defined baselines and measurement periods.
- **Risk-score-tied subscriptions**: Pricing tied to an independently measured risk posture score, where improvement reduces the fee and degradation increases it.
- **Shared savings models**: Arrangements where a portion of the vendor's fee is tied to demonstrated cost avoidance or efficiency improvements for the buyer.
- **Incident severity caps**: Commercial terms that cap the buyer's financial exposure for incidents above a defined severity threshold.

Our assessment found that success and outcome-linked fee structures represent the weakest pricing dimension in the MDR market by a wide margin, scoring less than half of subscription transparency. The typical MDR vendor has no outcome-linked pricing mechanism whatsoever. Even among the top performers on this dimension, adoption is in early stages. The few providers showing meaningful progress are large consultancies with composable models, not pureplay MDR firms.

analysis_sections.title: Why Outcome-Based Pricing Adoption Lags So Far Behind
analysis_sections.body:
Several structural and organizational factors explain the sluggish adoption of outcome-based pricing, despite clear buyer demand:

**1. Lack of measurement infrastructure.** Outcome-based pricing requires metrics that both parties trust. Most MDR providers lack the telemetry, benchmarking, and reporting infrastructure to measure and attribute outcomes with enough rigor to tie commercial terms to them. Without normalized baselines for detection time, response time, incident frequency, or coverage breadth, outcome commitments cannot be quantified.

**2. Revenue predictability addiction.** Subscription-only models provide smooth, predictable revenue streams that are rewarded by investors and simplify financial planning. Outcome-based components introduce variability into the revenue model, which finance teams and boards resist. Roughly two-thirds of providers remain subscription-only, and their overall pricing maturity lags well behind composable vendors, indicating that the subscription model itself constrains pricing sophistication.

**3. Insufficient AI capability to underwrite guarantees.** Outcome-based pricing requires confidence in delivery. A vendor cannot offer a breach warranty or response time guarantee without the AI-driven detection and response capabilities to consistently achieve them. Our data shows this directly: vendors with advanced AI influence score roughly double the outcome-linked pricing adoption of their minimal-tier counterparts. AI maturity is the prerequisite for outcome pricing.

**4. Misaligned organizational incentives.** In many MDR providers, pricing decisions are owned by finance or product management teams that optimize for margin protection, not by security operations teams that understand what outcomes are achievable. This creates a structural disconnect where the people closest to delivery have the least influence on commercial model design.

**5. Fear of accountability.** Outcome-linked pricing makes vendor performance transparent and has real consequences. If a provider commits to a rapid response time on critical incidents and fails, the financial penalty is immediate and visible. Many vendors prefer the opacity of flat-rate subscriptions where poor performance is masked and contract renewals are a commercial negotiation rather than a performance evaluation.

**6. Legacy contract structures.** Existing multi-year subscription contracts create inertia. Migrating a large installed base from flat-rate subscriptions to outcome-linked models requires renegotiating hundreds of contracts, retraining sales teams, and rebuilding billing systems, a transformation most vendors underestimate.

analysis_sections.title: AI Is Changing the Cost Equation, but Buyers Aren't Seeing It
analysis_sections.body:
Agentic AI is sharply reducing the per-incident cost of MDR service delivery. Automated triage, AI-accelerated threat hunting, machine-driven response playbooks, and predictive detection are enabling vendors to handle more volume with fewer human analysts. This should, in theory, create a natural transition toward efficiency-sharing or outcome-aligned pricing: the vendor delivers more value at lower cost, and the buyer shares in that efficiency gain.

Instead, most vendors are capturing the AI efficiency dividend entirely as margin improvement. Usage-based alignment remains weak across the market, meaning most vendors have no mechanism for buyers to see, let alone benefit from, AI-driven cost reductions. The buyer pays the same subscription fee whether their incidents are handled by a senior analyst spending hours on manual investigation or by an AI agent that resolves the same alert in minutes.

This will not hold. As buyers become more informed about AI capabilities and costs, they will demand transparency into how AI efficiency affects what they pay. The roughly 20% of vendors in the advanced AI influence tier are beginning to build this transparency through AI workload dashboards, cost-per-incident reporting, and graduated pricing tiers that reflect AI utilization. These vendors are not more generous; they are more strategic. By sharing the efficiency dividend early, they build a competitive advantage rooted in trust, transparency, and demonstrable value that subscription-only providers cannot replicate.

analysis_sections.title: The Composable Model Imperative
analysis_sections.body:
The data reveals a clear structural prerequisite for pricing model evolution: composability. Vendors with composable pricing models, where buyers can assemble service packages from modular components, consistently outscore subscription-only providers across every pricing dimension. The gap is widest on outcome-linked pricing, where composable vendors score nearly double their subscription-only counterparts.

This is not coincidental. Outcome-based pricing components cannot be bolted onto a flat-rate subscription. They require the architectural flexibility to price different service layers differently: a base detection fee, a response orchestration component, an outcome guarantee overlay, a shared-savings mechanism. Each layer has distinct cost drivers, risk profiles, and measurement requirements.

Roughly 30% of the market has adopted composable models and is positioned to add outcome-linked components over time. The remaining two-thirds face a structural rebuild before outcomes can even be priced. As AI continues to change how MDR services are delivered, this divide will widen into a lasting competitive gap.

reports.background:
The managed detection and response (MDR) market has seen considerable consolidation and commoditization pressure over the past three years. As core detection and response capabilities have become table stakes, pricing has emerged as a primary competitive battleground and a key indicator of vendor positioning.

This assessment evaluated MDR service providers across six pricing dimensions: subscription transparency, usage-based alignment, fixed delivery pricing, success and outcome fees, composability and model maturity, and pricing-to-outcomes alignment. Each dimension was scored on a standardized scale based on evidence from vendor documentation, publicly available pricing information, and contracted engagement terms.

The overall market average pricing maturity places the MDR market in the "developing" stage. Subscription transparency is the only dimension that has reached a reasonable level of maturity, reflecting an industry that has made progress in publishing clear tier structures and feature sets. Every other dimension falls well short, with the two outcome-related dimensions, success and outcome fees and pricing-to-outcomes alignment, trailing by the widest margin.

The AI enrichment layer, which assesses how AI operational maturity influences pricing model sophistication, reveals that no vendors have reached the most advanced tier, roughly 20% are at significant maturity, about half sit at an emerging level, and close to 30% remain minimal. The market has not yet translated AI investment into commercial model innovation at scale.
reports.impact:
The implications of this pricing maturity deficit are direct and practical for both MDR providers and the organizations they serve.

**For MDR vendors,** the inability to articulate and deliver outcome-based pricing will become a serious competitive problem within the next two to three years. As AI-first vendors use efficiency gains to fund outcome guarantees (breach warranties, response time commitments, risk-score-linked pricing), providers that cannot match these commercial structures will compete solely on price and feature lists. This is a losing position in a commoditizing market. The pricing sophistication gap between AI-mature and AI-minimal vendors is already visible in win rates and retention, and it will grow.

**For buyers,** the slow adoption of outcome-based pricing means they continue to bear the full risk of poor vendor performance. A subscription-only MDR contract provides no financial consequence if the vendor fails to detect a breach, responds slowly, or delivers inconsistent coverage. Buyers should actively seek vendors willing to put commercial terms against measurable outcomes, and treat a vendor's refusal to do so as a signal about their confidence in their own capabilities.

**For the broader cybersecurity services market,** the MDR pricing evolution is a leading indicator of a market-wide shift. As AI transforms cost structures across managed security services, the pressure for outcome-aligned pricing will extend to SOC-as-a-Service, vulnerability management, and security consulting. Vendors that develop outcome-based commercial capabilities in MDR will have a transferable advantage across their portfolio.

Platform MDR providers are best positioned to lead this transition. Their technology platform investments provide the telemetry infrastructure needed to measure outcomes, and their AI adoption is creating the efficiency surplus needed to fund outcome guarantees. Incident response-enhanced MDR providers show the highest pricing maturity but may be constrained by their smaller scale and incident-dependent revenue streams.

Pureplay MDR providers face the most significant challenge. Without the AI capability to underwrite outcome commitments or the platform telemetry to measure them, pureplay vendors risk being squeezed between platform providers offering outcome guarantees at competitive prices and niche specialists offering deep expertise at premium rates.
reports.conclusion:
The MDR pricing picture shows a market in transition that has not yet arrived. Subscription transparency is reasonably mature, but outcome-based pricing, the dimension that matters most to buyers, is essentially absent. The vast majority of vendors show little to no adoption of success and outcome-linked fee structures; the market is not incrementally behind, it has barely started.

AI adoption is the single most predictive variable in pricing model sophistication. The gap between AI-mature and AI-minimal vendors is substantial across every pricing dimension and is most pronounced on outcome alignment, where advanced vendors score more than double their least-mature counterparts. AI capability is not just correlated with pricing innovation; it enables it. Vendors cannot credibly commit to outcome-based pricing without the AI-driven detection, response, and measurement capabilities to consistently deliver against those commitments.

The path forward requires three parallel investments: AI capability maturity (to underwrite outcome guarantees), pricing architecture modernization (from subscription-only to composable), and measurement infrastructure (to enable transparent, trust-based outcome metrics). Vendors that treat pricing model evolution as a finance exercise rather than a capability development effort will find themselves unable to compete as the market matures.

Product leaders should not wait for buyer pressure to force this transition. The vendors that move first, establishing outcome-linked commercial terms while competitors stick with subscription-only models, will set the standard for what "good" looks like and make it harder for followers to catch up. AI maturity enables pricing innovation, pricing innovation enables competitive differentiation, and competitive differentiation determines long-term market position.

analysis_sections.title: The SOAR-to-AI Swap: Why Product Teams Are Building the Wrong Thing
analysis_sections.body:
The dominant product investment pattern in MDR over the past 18 months is straightforward: replace SOAR-based playbook automation with AI/ML-driven orchestration. Vendors are rewriting triage logic to use machine learning classifiers instead of rule trees, replacing manual investigation workflows with AI-assisted enrichment, and swapping static response playbooks with AI-driven decision engines.

The problem is not that this work is bad engineering. It often reduces mean time to triage, lowers false positive rates, and improves analyst efficiency. The problem is that none of these improvements show up in the commercial model. The vendor still sells a flat subscription. The customer still pays per-seat or per-endpoint. The AI reduces the vendor's cost of delivery without changing what the customer experiences commercially.

Our data makes this visible. Emerging-tier vendors (those that have shipped AI features but not connected them to pricing) score only marginally higher on pricing maturity than minimal-tier vendors who have no meaningful AI at all. By contrast, vendors at the advanced tier, who built AI in ways that change their commercial model, score a full point higher than the emerging tier.

The takeaway for product leaders: shipping better AI is not enough. The AI has to change what you can sell.

analysis_sections.title: Product Architecture Is the Real Pricing Bottleneck
analysis_sections.body:
When product leaders ask why their pricing team can't offer composable or outcome-linked models, the answer is almost always product architecture. Consider what outcome-based pricing requires:

- **Normalized outcome metrics**: detection time, response time, detection coverage, incident frequency. These need to be measured per-customer, with baselines, trending, and attribution. Most MDR products measure aggregate operational metrics for internal use, not per-customer outcome metrics for commercial use.

- **Modular service boundaries**: To price detection separately from response, or base service separately from outcome guarantees, the product must actually deliver these as separable components with independent SLAs and telemetry.

- **Confidence scoring**: To underwrite a response time guarantee or breach warranty, the product needs to express detection and response confidence in a way that actuaries (or at least finance teams) can model.

- **Usage telemetry**: To offer usage-based pricing components, the product needs metering infrastructure that tracks AI workload volume, incident complexity, and resource consumption at a per-customer level.

Roughly two-thirds of vendors lack these capabilities. Their product delivers MDR as a monolithic pipeline: alerts go in, validated incidents and responses come out. There is no internal boundary where a pricing team could insert a usage meter, an outcome metric, or a modular component boundary. The product architecture dictates subscription-only pricing, regardless of what the commercial team wants.

The composable-model vendors have invested in product decomposition. Their roughly 30% pricing maturity premium over subscription-only providers is not because their sales team is more creative. It's because their product team gave pricing something to work with.

analysis_sections.title: AI Efficiency Gains Are Going to Margin, Not to Product Differentiation
analysis_sections.body:
Product teams are improving operational efficiency with AI and reporting this as a product success. Triage time is down. Analyst-to-incident ratios are up. Cost per incident is falling. These are real improvements.

But from a product strategy perspective, efficiency gains that go entirely to margin are a wasted competitive asset. Vendors at the advanced AI tier are using AI efficiency data as product features: customer-facing AI workload dashboards, cost-per-incident trending reports, and transparent efficiency metrics that customers can see. These features become the foundation for pricing innovation because they give customers something to pay for (or pay less for) based on AI performance.

Usage-based alignment remains weak across the market. Most products do not expose any AI efficiency data to customers in a way that could support pricing changes. The product team captures the efficiency, finance captures the margin, and the customer sees no difference.

Product leaders who want to compete on pricing in 2027-2028 need to treat AI efficiency visibility as a product feature on the roadmap, not a back-office operational metric. The vendors who share this data with customers are building trust and commercial leverage that subscription-only competitors cannot match.

analysis_sections.title: The 12-Month Product Investment Window
analysis_sections.body:
The gap between the top pricing leaders and the market average is substantial and growing. The product decisions that enabled the leaders' pricing models were made 12-18 months before those models shipped. This means the investment window for mid-market vendors is now.

A realistic 12-month product roadmap for pricing enablement should target four milestones:

**Months 1-3: Outcome measurement infrastructure.** Ship per-customer detection and response time tracking, normalized baselines, and trending. This is the prerequisite for any outcome-linked pricing component and the capability most vendors lack.

**Months 3-6: Service decomposition.** Identify 2-3 modular boundaries in the MDR pipeline (e.g., base detection, response orchestration, threat hunting) and instrument each with independent telemetry and SLA surfaces.

**Months 6-9: AI efficiency exposure.** Build a customer-facing AI workload dashboard that shows AI triage rates, automation percentages, and cost efficiency trends. This becomes the pricing team's tool for usage-based and efficiency-sharing conversations.

**Months 9-12: First outcome-linked capability.** Ship a response time guarantee with service credits (or similar) on at least one tier, backed by the measurement infrastructure from months 1-3 and the AI detection confidence from the existing pipeline.

This sequence moves a vendor from the vast majority stuck at minimal outcome adoption to a position where outcome-linked pricing is at least available. The product investment is concrete, sequenced, and directly tied to commercial model impact.

analysis_sections.title: What Outcome-Based Pricing Actually Means, and Why the Market Gets It Wrong
analysis_sections.body:
"Outcome-based pricing" has become an MDR marketing fixture. Vendors cite SLA response times or uptime guarantees as evidence of outcome alignment. This misrepresents the concept.

True outcome-based pricing creates a direct financial link between what the buyer pays and the measurable security outcomes delivered. Commercial terms adjust based on metrics that matter: threat detection and containment speed, whether the attack surface is shrinking, incident frequency and severity trends, and cost of security per unit of business value.

Practical forms include:

- **Breach warranties**: Financial guarantees that pay out if a covered breach occurs, underwritten by vendor detection and response confidence.
- **Performance-linked fee adjustments**: Pricing that flexes based on achieved detection and response time improvements against defined baselines.
- **Risk-score-tied subscriptions**: Pricing linked to independently measured risk posture, where improvement reduces the fee.
- **Shared savings models**: Fees tied to demonstrated cost avoidance or efficiency improvements.
- **Incident severity caps**: Terms capping buyer financial exposure for incidents above a defined severity threshold.

Success and outcome-linked fees scored as the weakest pricing dimension by a wide margin, nearly half the score of subscription transparency. The typical vendor has no outcome-linked mechanism at all. Even the top performers on this dimension barely reach the midpoint of the scale. The few vendors scoring well are large consultancies with composable models, not pureplay MDR providers.

analysis_sections.title: Why Outcome-Based Pricing Adoption Lags
analysis_sections.body:
Several structural factors explain sluggish adoption despite buyer demand:

**1. No measurement infrastructure.** Most MDR providers lack the telemetry, benchmarking, and reporting to measure and attribute outcomes rigorously enough for commercial commitments. Without normalized detection time, response time, incident frequency, or coverage baselines, outcome commitments cannot be quantified.

**2. Revenue predictability addiction.** Subscription models provide smooth, predictable revenue rewarded by investors. Outcome components introduce variability that finance teams resist. Roughly two-thirds of vendors remain subscription-only, consistently underperforming composable vendors on pricing maturity.

**3. Insufficient AI capability to underwrite guarantees.** A vendor cannot offer breach warranties or response time guarantees without AI-driven capabilities to consistently deliver. Vendors with advanced AI influence score meaningfully higher on outcome-linked pricing than those at the minimal tier. AI maturity is the prerequisite.

**4. Misaligned organizational incentives.** Pricing decisions are often owned by finance or product management teams optimizing for margin protection, not by security operations teams that understand achievable outcomes.

**5. Fear of accountability.** Outcome-linked pricing makes vendor performance transparent with real consequences. Many vendors prefer the opacity of flat-rate subscriptions where poor performance is masked.

**6. Legacy contract structures.** Multi-year subscription contracts create inertia. Migration requires renegotiating hundreds of contracts, retraining sales, and rebuilding billing systems.

analysis_sections.title: AI Is Changing the Cost Equation, but Buyers Aren't Seeing It
analysis_sections.body:
Agentic AI is sharply reducing per-incident MDR delivery costs. Automated triage, AI-accelerated threat hunting, machine-driven response playbooks, and predictive detection enable more volume with fewer analysts. This should create a natural transition toward efficiency-sharing or outcome-aligned pricing.

Instead, most vendors capture the AI efficiency dividend as margin improvement. Usage-based alignment remains one of the weaker dimensions; most vendors have no mechanism for buyers to see or benefit from AI-driven cost reductions. The buyer pays the same subscription whether incidents are handled by a senior analyst spending hours on manual investigation or an AI agent resolving the same alert in minutes.

This will not hold. As buyers learn about AI capabilities and costs, they will demand transparency. Vendors with advanced AI influence are building this through AI workload dashboards, cost-per-incident reporting, and graduated tiers reflecting AI utilization. They are not more generous; they are more strategic. Sharing the efficiency dividend early builds competitive advantage rooted in trust and demonstrable value that subscription-only providers cannot replicate.

analysis_sections.title: The Composable Model Imperative
analysis_sections.body:
The data reveals a clear structural prerequisite for pricing evolution: composability. Vendors with composable pricing models consistently outscore subscription-only providers across every pricing dimension. The gap is widest on outcome-linked pricing, where composable vendors score nearly double their subscription-only counterparts.

Outcome-based pricing cannot be bolted onto a flat-rate subscription. It requires architectural flexibility to price different service layers differently: a base detection fee, a response orchestration component, an outcome guarantee overlay, a shared-savings mechanism. Each layer has distinct cost drivers, risk profiles, and measurement requirements.

Roughly a third of vendors have adopted composable models and are positioned to add outcome-linked components over time. The two-thirds still operating subscription-only face a structural rebuild before outcomes can even be priced. As AI continues reshaping MDR delivery, this divide will widen into a lasting competitive gap.

analysis_sections.title: The SOAR-to-AI Swap: Why Product Teams Are Building the Wrong Thing
analysis_sections.body:
The dominant MDR product investment over the past 18 months: replace SOAR-based playbook automation with AI/ML-driven orchestration. Vendors rewrite triage logic to use ML classifiers, replace manual investigation with AI-assisted enrichment, and swap static playbooks with AI decision engines.

The engineering is often sound, reducing triage time, lowering false positive rates, and improving analyst efficiency. The problem: none of these improvements appear in the commercial model. The vendor still sells a flat subscription. The customer still pays per-seat or per-endpoint. AI reduces the vendor's delivery cost without changing the customer's commercial experience.

The data confirms this. Emerging-tier vendors (AI features shipped but not connected to pricing) score only marginally above minimal-tier vendors (no meaningful AI in pricing). The advanced-tier vendors, who built AI in ways changing their commercial model, outperform emerging by a wide margin.

Shipping better AI is not enough. The AI has to change what you can sell.

analysis_sections.title: Product Architecture Is the Real Pricing Bottleneck
analysis_sections.body:
When product leaders ask why pricing cannot offer composable or outcome-linked models, the answer is almost always product architecture. Outcome-based pricing requires:

- **Normalized outcome metrics**: Detection time, response time, detection coverage, incident frequency, measured per-customer with baselines, trending, and attribution. Most products measure aggregate operational metrics for internal use, not per-customer outcome metrics for commercial use.

- **Modular service boundaries**: To price detection separately from response, or base service from outcome guarantees, the product must deliver these as separable components with independent SLAs and telemetry.

- **Confidence scoring**: To underwrite response time guarantees or breach warranties, the product needs detection and response confidence expressed in a way finance teams can model.

- **Usage telemetry**: Per-customer metering of AI workload volume, incident complexity, and resource consumption.

The majority of vendors lack these capabilities. Their product delivers MDR as a monolithic pipeline: alerts in, incidents and responses out. No internal boundary exists where a pricing team could insert a usage meter, outcome metric, or component boundary. Architecture dictates subscription-only pricing.

The composable-model vendors invested in decomposition. Their pricing premium over subscription-only comes from product giving pricing something to work with.

analysis_sections.title: What the Top Pricing Leaders Did Differently, a Product Perspective

The top vendors by pricing maturity share common product architecture patterns that directly enabled their commercial models:

**Modular telemetry from day one.** They built metering and measurement as product infrastructure, not reporting afterthoughts. Per-customer outcome tracking, AI utilization metrics, and detection confidence scoring are product features with APIs, not dashboard widgets.

**Deliberate service decomposition.** They separated their pipeline into independently deliverable, independently measurable components. This was a product architecture decision, not a pricing team request.

**AI capability mapped to commercial enablement.** Their AI roadmaps included specific pricing model milestones: "this detection confidence threshold enables this SLA tier" or "this automation level enables this consumption-based component."

**Outcome measurement as product truth.** They automated outcome baselining, trending, and attribution, then exposed these as customer-facing metrics. When pricing offered response time guarantees, the product already measured response time per-customer with statistical rigor.

These decisions were made 12-18 months before the pricing models shipped. Product leaders replicate this by embedding pricing-enablement milestones in product roadmaps now, not after the pricing team asks.

**Stage 2: AI-Enabled Telemetry.** AI generates per-customer measurement infrastructure: workload volume tracking, detection confidence scoring, outcome baselining. Pricing impact: enables usage-based components and transparent efficiency reporting.

Pricing impact: enables composable pricing with independently priced modules.

**Stage 4: AI-Underwritten Outcome Guarantees.** AI detection and response confidence is high enough and measurable enough to underwrite commercial commitments: response time guarantees, detection coverage commitments, risk score improvement targets. Pricing impact: enables outcome-linked pricing components with financial mechanisms.

**Stage 5: AI-Native Commercial Model.** The full pricing model is architecturally dependent on AI capabilities: dynamic pricing based on real-time risk assessment, automated outcome measurement triggering pricing adjustments, AI-driven service optimization affecting what the customer pays. Pricing impact: transformative, creating a commercial model competitors cannot replicate without equivalent AI capability.

The top pricing leaders built measurement infrastructure, modular service boundaries, and AI-to-pricing pipelines into their product 12-18 months before shipping competitive pricing models. Product teams that treat pricing model support as a finance or sales concern will find their commercial teams unable to compete.

**For the market,** MDR pricing evolution is a leading indicator. As AI transforms cost structures across managed security services, outcome-aligned pricing pressure will extend to SOC-as-a-Service, vulnerability management, and security consulting.

Platform providers are best positioned. IR-enhanced providers have the highest pricing maturity but are constrained by scale. Pureplay providers face the greatest challenge without AI capability or platform telemetry for outcome commitments.
reports.conclusion:
MDR pricing is in transition but has not arrived. Subscription transparency is mature; outcome-based pricing is essentially absent. The vast majority of vendors show little to no adoption of outcome-linked fee structures.

AI adoption is the single most predictive variable. The gap between AI-mature and AI-minimal vendors, and wider divergence on outcome dimensions, confirm that AI capability enables pricing innovation. For product leaders, the critical realization is that this is a product problem: AI maturity, modular architecture, and measurement infrastructure must be built at the product level before commercial teams can act.

Three parallel product investments are required: AI capability maturity (to underwrite outcome guarantees), service architecture decomposition (from monolithic to composable), and measurement infrastructure (per-customer, API-accessible outcome metrics). Treating pricing evolution as a finance exercise rather than a product capability priority will leave vendors unable to compete.

Product leaders should act now. The 12-18 month lag between product architecture decisions and commercial model capability means investments made today determine competitiveness in 2027-2028.
