reports.title: Market Insight: MDR Vendors Cannot Price Outcomes They Cannot Measure — AI Changes That
reports.summary: 84% of MDR vendors score ≤2 on outcome maturity. The barrier is not commercial will but measurement infrastructure. AI enables six metric categories that make outcome-based pricing viable for the first time.
reports.spa: By 2028, MDR vendors that deploy AI-powered outcome measurement platforms covering at least four of six metric categories (speed, autonomy, coverage, quality, resource, and impact) will capture 60% of new outcome-linked contract value. Vendors without normalized, per-customer AI-generated outcome metrics by 2027 will be structurally unable to compete on outcome-based commercial terms.

findings.header: F1: The outcome metrics gap is the binding constraint — vendors cannot price what they cannot measure.
findings.body: Of 98 MDR vendors assessed, 82 (84%) score at outcome maturity level 2 or below. Only 2 vendors reach level 4 (Accenture Security, Deloitte Cyber — both large consultancies, not pureplay MDR). Zero vendors reach level 5 (Outcome-Native). The PRC-SUC dimension averages 2.25/5.0 and PRC-OUT averages 2.42/5.0, but these scores are not limited by commercial reluctance. They are limited by the absence of measurement infrastructure. Vendors report willingness to explore outcome-based pricing in client conversations but lack the per-customer, normalized, attribution-capable metrics required to underwrite outcome commitments. The measurement gap is the root cause.

findings.header: F2: AI creates six outcome metric categories that were previously unmeasurable at commercial-grade fidelity.
findings.body: The MDR schema defines six ROI measurement categories: Speed (MTTD/MTTR reduction), Autonomy (% incidents resolved without human intervention), Coverage (telemetry source expansion), Quality (false positive rate trend, hallucination incidents), Resource (analyst time freed), and Impact (damage prevention, regulatory penalty avoidance). Before AI, measuring these at per-customer granularity with enough rigor to back commercial commitments was impractical. AI-driven detection pipelines, automated triage, and machine-generated attribution now make it feasible to produce these metrics continuously, per-customer, with baselines and trending. This is the structural change that makes outcome-based pricing viable.

findings.header: F3: Speed metrics (MTTD/MTTR) are the most mature but least differentiating outcome category.
findings.body: MTTD and MTTR are the metrics most commonly cited in vendor marketing and buyer RFPs. Among the 16 vendors at outcome maturity ≥3, all 16 publish some form of MTTD/MTTR data. However, speed metrics alone do not differentiate: they are easily gamed (by narrowing detection scope to reduce MTTD) and tell buyers nothing about coverage breadth, risk reduction, or business impact. Vendors building outcome pricing exclusively around speed are optimizing for the metric buyers already expect rather than the metrics that drive retention and expansion. Speed is necessary but not sufficient.

findings.header: F4: Autonomy metrics — AI resolution without human intervention — are the highest-value differentiator but the least measured.
findings.body: The percentage of incidents fully resolved by AI without human analyst involvement is the metric most directly tied to AI's commercial value proposition: it quantifies the efficiency dividend buyers should share. Yet fewer than 10 of 98 vendors publish autonomy rates at the per-customer level. Significant-tier AI vendors (19 providers, avg outcome maturity 2.58) are beginning to track this internally, but even they rarely expose it commercially. Autonomy metrics are the most powerful lever for outcome-based pricing because they make AI's value visible and attributable — the prerequisite for tying price to performance.

findings.header: F5: Quality and coverage metrics are ignored despite being the outcomes buyers value most after a breach.
findings.body: Post-breach client inquiries consistently prioritize two questions: Was the threat in scope (coverage)? Was the alert prioritized correctly (quality)? Yet coverage breadth (telemetry sources monitored, attack surface mapped) and quality trends (false positive rate, alert fidelity, detection confidence scoring) are the least developed metric categories across the MDR market. Only composable-model vendors (27 providers, avg outcome maturity 2.44) show meaningful investment in coverage and quality reporting. Subscription-only vendors (65 providers, avg outcome maturity 1.52) treat coverage as a static capability description rather than a measurable, improvable outcome.

findings.header: F6: AI maturity is the strongest predictor of outcome measurement capability — the gap is 1.47 points between tiers.
findings.body: Vendors at the Significant AI tier average outcome maturity of 2.58 versus 1.11 for Minimal-tier vendors — a 1.47-point gap on a 5-point scale. This is not coincidental. AI-mature vendors have the infrastructure to generate outcome metrics: their detection pipelines produce confidence scores, their response engines track resolution paths, their platforms measure per-customer telemetry coverage, and their automation tracks human-vs-machine attribution. Minimal-tier vendors lack every one of these capabilities. The implication is direct: investing in AI operational maturity is investing in outcome measurement capability, which is investing in the ability to price on outcomes.

recommendations.header: R1: Build an AI-powered outcome measurement platform as a first-class product feature, not a reporting afterthought. [Responds to F1, F2]
recommendations.body: The measurement infrastructure gap (F1) cannot be closed with better dashboards bolted onto existing products. Product teams must build a dedicated outcome measurement layer that ingests data from the detection and response pipeline and produces per-customer, normalized metrics across all six ROI categories identified in F2. This layer needs: (a) per-customer baselines established within 30 days of onboarding, (b) continuous metric computation with weekly and monthly trending, (c) attribution logic that separates AI-driven outcomes from analyst-driven outcomes, (d) API-accessible metrics that commercial teams can reference in contract terms. The two vendors at outcome maturity 4 (Accenture, Deloitte) both built dedicated measurement platforms rather than extending their operational dashboards. This is a product investment, not a BI project.

recommendations.header: R2: Sequence metric deployment starting with speed, then autonomy, then coverage and quality. [Responds to F3, F4, F5]
recommendations.body: While speed metrics alone do not differentiate (F3), they are the most tractable starting point because the raw data (detection and response timestamps) already exists in most MDR pipelines. The deployment sequence should be: Phase 1 (months 1-3): Normalize MTTD/MTTR per-customer with baselines and trending — this enables the first outcome-linked pricing component (e.g., MTTR guarantee with service credits). Phase 2 (months 3-6): Deploy autonomy metrics tracking AI-vs-human resolution attribution per customer — this makes the AI efficiency dividend visible and priceable (F4). Phase 3 (months 6-12): Instrument coverage breadth scoring (telemetry sources, attack surface mapped) and quality trending (false positive rates, detection confidence) — these are the metrics buyers value most post-breach (F5) and the hardest for competitors to replicate.

recommendations.header: R3: Develop composite outcome indices that combine multiple metric categories into commercially actionable scores. [Responds to F1, F3, F5]
recommendations.body: Individual metrics (MTTD, autonomy rate, false positive ratio) are necessary for transparency but insufficient for commercial structures. Vendors should develop composite outcome indices that combine metrics into a single score buyers and vendors can contract against. Examples: (a) a Detection Efficacy Index combining MTTD, false positive rate, and detection confidence, (b) a Response Value Index combining MTTR, autonomy rate, and containment completeness, (c) a Coverage Health Score combining telemetry breadth, attack surface coverage, and visibility gap trending. Composite indices solve the problem of gaming individual metrics (F3) and give commercial teams a defensible basis for outcome-linked pricing tiers. The index methodology should be transparent, auditable, and published.

recommendations.header: R4: Expose autonomy metrics as the primary AI-differentiated commercial lever. [Responds to F4, F6]
recommendations.body: The autonomy rate — percentage of incidents fully resolved by AI without human intervention — is the single metric that most directly connects AI investment to buyer value. Vendors at the Significant AI tier (F6) already have the pipeline to measure this but are not exposing it commercially. Product teams should: (a) Instrument every incident with a resolution-path tag (fully automated, AI-assisted, analyst-driven), (b) Compute per-customer autonomy rates weekly, (c) Expose these rates in customer reporting alongside the cost-per-incident implications, (d) Build pricing tiers where higher autonomy rates translate to lower per-incident costs or shared-savings mechanisms. This is the metric that converts the AI efficiency dividend from a vendor margin play into a buyer value proposition.

recommendations.header: R5: Tie metric maturity milestones to specific pricing model unlocks on a 12-month roadmap. [Responds to F1, F6]
recommendations.body: Each metric category, once measured at commercial grade, unlocks a specific pricing mechanism: Speed metrics unlock MTTR/MTTD guarantees with service credits. Autonomy metrics unlock efficiency-sharing and cost-per-incident pricing. Coverage metrics unlock risk-score-tied subscriptions. Quality metrics unlock detection confidence warranties. Resource metrics unlock analyst-time-saved rebates. Impact metrics unlock breach warranties and damage-cap guarantees. Product teams should map their measurement deployment sequence (R2) to explicit pricing model milestones, with commercial teams involved in defining the thresholds, financial mechanisms, and contract language for each unlock. The 1.47-point outcome maturity gap between Significant and Minimal AI tiers (F6) demonstrates that AI investment without commercial roadmap alignment produces measurement capability that never reaches the customer.

analysis_sections.title: The Measurement Infrastructure Deficit: Why 84% of Vendors Cannot Price on Outcomes (F1 → R1)
analysis_sections.body:
Outcome-based pricing requires a capability most MDR vendors do not have: the ability to measure, normalize, baseline, and attribute security outcomes at the per-customer level with enough rigor to back commercial commitments.

Consider what a simple MTTR guarantee requires. The vendor must: (a) define MTTR consistently across incident types and severity levels, (b) establish a customer-specific baseline within the first 30 days, (c) measure MTTR continuously with automated time-stamping across detection, triage, investigation, and containment, (d) attribute improvements to specific capabilities (AI triage, human investigation, automated response), and (e) report these metrics in a format the customer can independently verify.

Now multiply that across six metric categories — speed, autonomy, coverage, quality, resource, and impact — and the infrastructure requirement becomes clear. This is not a dashboard. It is a measurement platform that sits alongside the detection-and-response pipeline and produces commercially grade metrics as a primary output.

The 82 vendors at outcome maturity ≤2 lack this infrastructure entirely. Their operational metrics are aggregate, not per-customer. Their baselines are internal benchmarks, not contractual references. Their attribution logic does not separate AI-driven outcomes from analyst-driven outcomes. They can tell you their average MTTD across all customers; they cannot tell Customer A that their MTTD improved 34% this quarter, driven primarily by AI-automated triage of identity-based alerts, with a projected annual risk reduction of $2.1M.

The two vendors at outcome maturity 4 — Accenture Security and Deloitte Cyber — both invested in dedicated outcome measurement platforms. These are not MDR dashboards with extra charts. They are standalone measurement engines that ingest telemetry from the detection pipeline, compute per-customer metrics, maintain baselines, and produce the attribution data required for outcome-linked contracts. Both vendors report that building this platform took 12-18 months and required collaboration between product engineering, data science, and commercial teams.

This is the investment the market has not made. And until it does, outcome-based pricing will remain aspirational.

analysis_sections.title: The Six Metric Categories: What AI Makes Measurable for the First Time (F2 → R2, R3)
analysis_sections.body:
The MDR schema's ROI Measurement Framework identifies six KPI categories. AI transforms each from an operational estimate to a commercially measurable outcome.

**Speed Metrics: MTTD/MTTR Reduction**
Before AI: Measured manually with inconsistent definitions and self-reported timestamps. After AI: Automated pipeline instrumentation produces sub-second precision timing across every phase — alert generation, enrichment, triage, investigation, containment, remediation. AI enables per-customer, per-incident-type MTTD/MTTR with consistent definitions and tamper-resistant measurement. This is the most mature category and the natural starting point.

**Autonomy Metrics: % Incidents Resolved Without Human Intervention**
Before AI: Not measurable — all incidents required human involvement. After AI: Fully automated triage-to-containment workflows produce clear human/machine attribution. Every incident can be tagged as fully automated, AI-assisted, or analyst-driven. Per-customer autonomy rates become a key indicator of AI's delivered value and the foundation for efficiency-sharing pricing.

**Coverage Metrics: Telemetry Source Expansion and Attack Surface Mapping**
Before AI: Static capability descriptions (we monitor endpoint, network, cloud). After AI: Dynamic coverage scoring that measures actual telemetry ingestion, identifies visibility gaps, and tracks coverage breadth over time. AI-driven asset discovery and attack surface mapping turn coverage from a checkbox into a measurable, improvable metric.

**Quality Metrics: False Positive Rate Trend and Detection Confidence**
Before AI: False positive rates tracked internally without consistent methodology. After AI: Detection confidence scoring on every alert, false positive rate trending per customer, and — critically — hallucination tracking for AI-generated detections. Quality metrics measured by AI become the basis for detection efficacy guarantees.

**Resource Metrics: Analyst Time Freed**
Before AI: Estimated based on headcount ratios. After AI: Precise measurement of analyst time per incident, comparison against pre-AI baselines, and per-customer tracking of how AI automation affects internal security team workload. For customers who maintain internal SOC teams alongside MDR, this metric directly quantifies the vendor's resource impact.

**Impact Metrics: Damage Prevention, Regulatory Penalty Avoidance**
Before AI: Impossible to measure prospectively; assessed only post-incident. After AI: Predictive risk scoring, automated attack path analysis, and AI-driven threat modeling enable prospective impact estimation. While still the most complex category to measure at commercial grade, AI-driven risk quantification is advancing rapidly. Impact metrics are the eventual foundation for breach warranties and damage-cap guarantees.

The sequencing matters. Speed metrics are the foundation (readily measurable, universally understood). Autonomy metrics are the AI differentiator (directly link AI capability to commercial value). Coverage and quality are the retention drivers (address the questions buyers ask after incidents). Resource and impact are the advanced metrics that enable the most sophisticated pricing structures.

analysis_sections.title: The Speed Metric Trap: Why MTTD/MTTR Alone Will Not Sustain Outcome Pricing (F3 → R3)
analysis_sections.body:
Every MDR vendor that ventures into outcome-based pricing starts with the same metric: MTTR. It is measurable, familiar to buyers, and maps directly to a simple pricing mechanism (miss the MTTR target, pay a service credit). But MTTD/MTTR as sole outcome metrics create three problems that will undermine outcome pricing efforts:

**Problem 1: Scope Gaming.** A vendor can dramatically improve MTTD by narrowing detection scope. If you only detect threats you are already good at finding, your mean detection time looks excellent — but coverage gaps widen. Three of the top-10 vendors by MTTD performance show declining coverage breadth scores quarter-over-quarter, suggesting this pattern is already emerging. Outcome pricing built solely on speed incentivizes vendors to reduce scope to protect margins.

**Problem 2: Severity Masking.** Average MTTD/MTTR across all incidents obscures the metric that matters most: time to detect and respond to high-severity, novel threats. A vendor with a 5-minute average MTTR that takes 4 hours on critical incidents is delivering poor outcomes that the average conceals. Without severity-weighted speed metrics — which require the quality and coverage metrics from other categories — speed benchmarks give false confidence.

**Problem 3: Commoditization.** As AI improves across the market, MTTD/MTTR will converge. When every vendor can guarantee a 15-minute MTTR on standard incidents, speed ceases to differentiate. The vendors that built outcome pricing exclusively around speed will find their commercial model commoditized alongside the metric.

The solution is composite indices (R3) that combine speed with quality, coverage, and autonomy. A Detection Efficacy Index that weights MTTD by detection confidence and scope breadth is far more defensible commercially than raw MTTD alone. A Response Value Index that weights MTTR by containment completeness and autonomy rate captures value that speed alone misses.

Speed metrics are the starting point, not the destination. Vendors that treat them as the destination will find their outcome pricing advantage eroded within 18-24 months.

analysis_sections.title: Autonomy as Commercial Currency: Making AI's Value Visible and Priceable (F4 → R4)
analysis_sections.body:
The autonomy rate — the percentage of security incidents fully resolved from detection through containment without any human analyst intervention — is the metric the MDR market needs but is not yet willing to publish.

Consider the commercial implications. If a vendor's AI resolves 65% of incidents autonomously for Customer A, that customer is paying the same subscription fee but receiving fundamentally different value than Customer B, where only 30% of incidents are auto-resolved. Customer A's security team spends less time on MDR-covered incidents, Customer A's mean time to respond is faster, and Customer A's risk exposure during the detection-to-containment window is lower.

Today, neither customer knows their autonomy rate. The vendor captures the efficiency as margin. This is the core of the AI efficiency dividend problem identified in the existing pricing report — and autonomy metrics are the specific mechanism to solve it.

For vendors, publishing autonomy rates is uncomfortable for two reasons. First, low rates expose the gap between AI marketing and AI reality. A vendor claiming "AI-powered MDR" with a 15% autonomy rate faces awkward questions. Second, high rates raise buyer expectations for price reductions: if AI is doing most of the work, why is the subscription fee unchanged?

Both concerns are real but manageable — and the alternative (continuing to hide the metric) is untenable. As AI transparency expectations increase across enterprise software, the MDR market will face the same pressure. The vendors that voluntarily publish autonomy metrics first will earn buyer trust and set the narrative, while laggards will have it imposed on them through RFP requirements and analyst evaluations.

The commercial model for autonomy metrics is straightforward: graduated pricing where higher autonomy rates either reduce per-incident costs (cost-sharing) or are reinvested in advanced threat hunting and proactive coverage (value-added). The 19 Significant-tier AI vendors already have the pipeline to compute autonomy rates. The product decision is whether to expose this data to customers and build pricing around it. The data strongly suggests they should: Significant-tier vendors average 2.58 outcome maturity versus 1.11 for Minimal tier. The infrastructure is there. The commercial decision is not.

analysis_sections.title: Coverage and Quality: The Post-Breach Metrics That Should Drive Pre-Breach Pricing (F5 → R2, R3)
analysis_sections.body:
After every significant security incident, two questions dominate the forensic review: Was this threat within our detection coverage? And if we saw signals, did we correctly prioritize them? These are coverage and quality questions — and they are the metrics most absent from MDR outcome measurement.

**Coverage as a measurable outcome.** Most MDR vendors describe coverage in static terms: "We monitor endpoint, cloud, identity, and network telemetry." This tells the buyer nothing about actual coverage breadth — the percentage of the customer's attack surface where the vendor has active visibility. AI enables dynamic coverage scoring: automated asset discovery, continuous telemetry gap analysis, and coverage health trending that shows whether protection is expanding or contracting over time.

A Coverage Health Score that measures telemetry breadth (number of sources), depth (granularity per source), freshness (time since last data), and gap identification (known blind spots) turns coverage from a marketing claim into a measurable outcome. This metric becomes commercially powerful because it directly addresses the buyer's greatest fear: the threat the vendor didn't see because it came from an unmonitored surface.

Composable vendors (avg outcome maturity 2.44) are furthest ahead on coverage instrumentation, likely because their modular pricing already requires distinguishing what is and is not in scope. Subscription-only vendors (avg outcome maturity 1.52) bundle everything, which paradoxically makes coverage harder to measure — if "everything" is included, there is no mechanism to assess whether everything is actually monitored.

**Quality as a measurable outcome.** Detection quality encompasses false positive rates, alert fidelity, detection confidence scoring, and — uniquely for AI-driven MDR — hallucination tracking. AI detection pipelines can produce a confidence score for every alert, enabling quality to be measured continuously rather than assessed retroactively after missed threats.

A Detection Quality Index that trends false positive rates, tracks detection confidence distribution, and monitors hallucination incidents (AI-generated false detections with no underlying threat signal) gives buyers visibility into whether their MDR service is improving or degrading over time. This metric is commercially powerful for retention: a vendor that can demonstrate sustained quality improvement has a structural advantage in renewals that pure speed metrics cannot match.

The connection to pricing is direct. Coverage and quality metrics enable two pricing mechanisms that subscription-only models cannot support: risk-score-tied pricing (where improved coverage demonstrably lowers risk, justifying fee adjustments) and detection confidence warranties (where the vendor guarantees a minimum detection quality level backed by financial mechanisms).

analysis_sections.title: From Metrics to Money: Mapping Each Metric Category to a Pricing Mechanism (F1, F6 → R5)
analysis_sections.body:
The gap between measurement capability and commercial deployment is the final barrier. Even vendors that measure outcomes internally rarely connect those metrics to pricing structures. This section maps each metric category to the specific pricing mechanism it enables, providing product and commercial teams with a concrete translation layer.

**Speed Metrics → MTTR/MTTD Guarantees with Service Credits**
The simplest outcome-linked mechanism. The vendor commits to a per-customer MTTR target (e.g., <15 minutes for critical incidents), measured by the outcome platform, and pays service credits when missed. Requires: normalized per-customer MTTD/MTTR measurement, severity classification, and automated credit computation. Current market readiness: This mechanism is deployable now by the 16 vendors at outcome maturity ≥3.

**Autonomy Metrics → Efficiency-Sharing and Cost-Per-Incident Pricing**
As autonomy rates increase, the cost per incident decreases. Efficiency-sharing pricing passes a defined percentage of that cost reduction to the buyer, either as direct fee reductions or as reinvestment credits applied to advanced services. Requires: per-customer autonomy rate tracking, cost-per-incident modeling, and transparent AI attribution. Current market readiness: Significant-tier vendors (19) have the data; none have shipped this commercially.

**Coverage Metrics → Risk-Score-Tied Subscriptions**
Coverage Health Scores that demonstrate measurable risk reduction enable pricing that adjusts with risk posture. As coverage expands and visibility gaps close, the buyer's risk score improves, and the fee adjusts downward (or the vendor earns a performance bonus). Requires: dynamic coverage scoring, independent risk quantification, and agreed-upon scoring methodology. Current market readiness: 6-12 months of instrumentation required for most vendors.

**Quality Metrics → Detection Confidence Warranties**
A guarantee on minimum detection quality levels: maximum false positive rates, minimum detection confidence scores, and hallucination rate caps. If quality degrades below contracted thresholds, financial remedies apply. Requires: continuous quality scoring, per-customer trending, and agreed-upon quality definitions. Current market readiness: AI-mature vendors have the detection confidence infrastructure but have not commercialized it.

**Resource Metrics → Analyst-Time-Saved Rebates**
For customers with internal SOC teams, resource metrics quantify how much analyst time the MDR service saves. Pricing tied to resource metrics offers rebates or credits proportional to measured analyst time freed. Requires: integration with customer SOC tooling to measure internal analyst time, pre-engagement baseline, and ongoing tracking. Current market readiness: Complex; likely a Phase 3 capability.

**Impact Metrics → Breach Warranties and Damage-Cap Guarantees**
The most advanced mechanism: the vendor guarantees financial coverage for security incidents up to a defined cap, underwritten by their confidence in detection and response effectiveness. Requires: AI-driven risk quantification, actuarial modeling of breach cost distribution, and reinsurance partnerships. Current market readiness: Only the two level-4 vendors (Accenture, Deloitte) approach this capability, and both leverage their broader consulting risk practices.

The 12-month product roadmap should target the first three mechanisms (speed, autonomy, coverage) as deployable within a year, with quality mechanisms in development and resource/impact mechanisms in design. Each mechanism requires both the measurement capability (R1, R2) and the commercial framework (contract language, financial modeling, customer communication). Product and commercial teams must develop both in parallel.

reports.background:
This report extends the MDR pricing market insight by examining the specific outcome metrics that must underpin any viable outcome-based pricing model. The existing pricing assessment identified outcome-based pricing as the market's weakest dimension (PRC-SUC at 2.25/5.0, PRC-OUT at 2.42/5.0) and AI maturity as the strongest predictor of pricing sophistication. This report investigates why: the measurement infrastructure gap.

The analysis covers 98 MDR service providers assessed across outcome maturity (0-5 scale), six pricing dimensions, and AI pricing influence. The outcome maturity rating evaluates how directly a vendor's commercial terms connect to measurable client outcomes, from Input-Only (level 1: per-seat pricing with no outcome linkage) to Outcome-Native (level 5: entire model built around outcomes with balanced risk-sharing).

The MDR schema's ROI Measurement Framework defines six KPI categories — Speed, Autonomy, Coverage, Quality, Resource, and Impact — that constitute the metrics necessary for outcome-based pricing. This report assesses the market's capability to measure each category and maps measurement maturity to specific pricing mechanisms each enables.

Key baseline statistics: 84% of vendors score ≤2 on outcome maturity. Only 2 vendors (Accenture Security, Deloitte Cyber) reach level 4. Zero vendors reach level 5. The AI tier gap is decisive: Significant-tier vendors average 2.58 on outcome maturity versus 1.11 for Minimal-tier. Composable vendors average 2.44 versus 1.52 for subscription-only.
reports.impact:
The implications of the outcome metrics gap are structural and time-sensitive.

**For MDR product teams:** The measurement infrastructure described in this report is a 12-18 month build. Vendors that begin now will have deployable outcome measurement platforms by mid-2027. Vendors that delay face a compounding disadvantage: competitors with measurement platforms will set buyer expectations for metric transparency, outcome-linked contract terms, and performance visibility that latecomers cannot match without the same infrastructure investment.

**For MDR commercial teams:** Outcome-based pricing cannot be developed in isolation from product capability. The specific pricing mechanisms mapped in this report (MTTR guarantees, efficiency-sharing, risk-score-tied subscriptions, detection confidence warranties) each require specific measurement capabilities that product must build. Commercial and product teams should be developing these in parallel, with measurement milestones gating pricing model releases.

**For buyers:** The outcome maturity distribution (84% at ≤2) means most MDR vendors cannot currently deliver outcome-linked pricing even if asked. Buyers should evaluate vendors on their measurement infrastructure — can the vendor produce per-customer MTTD/MTTR with baselines and trending? Can they show autonomy rates? Can they demonstrate coverage health? These capabilities signal a vendor's readiness for outcome-based engagement regardless of their current pricing model.

**For AI-first MDR vendors:** The 1.47-point outcome maturity gap between Significant and Minimal AI tiers represents a window of competitive advantage that will narrow as the market matures. The priority is converting existing AI measurement capabilities (detection confidence, automated triage attribution, coverage mapping) into customer-facing metrics and pricing mechanisms before mid-market vendors replicate the infrastructure.

**For the broader cybersecurity services market:** The metric categories and pricing mechanisms described here are not MDR-specific. SOC-as-a-Service, vulnerability management, and managed CTEM providers face identical measurement gaps and will undergo similar outcome-pricing transitions. MDR vendors that develop outcome measurement platforms and associated commercial models will have transferable capabilities across their service portfolio.
reports.conclusion:
The MDR market's outcome-based pricing problem is, at its core, a measurement problem. Vendors are not avoiding outcome-based pricing because they prefer subscriptions — they are avoiding it because they cannot measure outcomes at the granularity, consistency, and rigor required to underwrite commercial commitments.

AI changes this equation fundamentally. The six metric categories defined in the ROI Measurement Framework — speed, autonomy, coverage, quality, resource, and impact — become commercially measurable for the first time when AI-driven detection and response pipelines produce the per-customer, attributed, baselined data these metrics require.

The data makes the priority order clear. Speed metrics are the foundation — measurable now, understood by buyers, and tied to the simplest pricing mechanisms. Autonomy metrics are the AI differentiator — the metric that makes AI's value visible and creates the commercial basis for efficiency-sharing. Coverage and quality metrics are the retention drivers — the outcomes buyers care about most when evaluating whether to renew. Resource and impact metrics are the advanced frontier — the basis for the most sophisticated pricing structures that only the most mature vendors will deploy.

The 1.47-point outcome maturity gap between Significant and Minimal AI tiers is the strongest signal in the data. It confirms that AI investment is not just correlated with outcome capability — it enables it. Vendors investing in AI without a parallel investment in AI-powered outcome measurement are building capability they cannot commercialize.

Product leaders should read this report as a product requirements document. The six metric categories are features. The composite indices are products. The pricing mechanisms are the commercial models those products enable. The 12-month roadmap from speed metrics to coverage and quality measurement is the minimum viable investment to participate in the outcome-based pricing transition.

The market will not wait. The two vendors at outcome maturity 4 are already contracting on outcome terms. The 14 vendors at level 3 are building measurement platforms. By 2028, outcome measurement capability will be a procurement requirement, not a differentiator. The question for every MDR vendor is whether they will have the metrics to compete.
